prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Trip.com Group Ltd" (ticker TCOM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TCOM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Trip.com Group Limited
result.industry: Online travel agency and travel search platforms
markets: China domestic hotel and flight booking (Ctrip, Qunar)
International online travel booking (Trip.com app in Asia, Europe and beyond)
Packaged tours and corporate travel management

mission.statement: to pursue the perfect trip for a better world
mission.source: Trip.com Group investor relations website, corporate profile
mission.plain: Make every trip go as smoothly as possible, and use travel to make the world a better place.

about.plain: Trip.com Group runs apps and websites where people book hotels, plane tickets, train tickets and holiday tours. In China its main app is Ctrip, and outside China it uses the Trip.com app. It also owns Skyscanner, a site that compares flight prices, and Qunar, another Chinese booking site. It earns a fee, called a commission, each time someone books through it.
about.customers: Millions of holiday and business travellers, mostly in China and Asia, plus companies that book work trips for their staff.
about.everyday: If you have compared cheap flights on Skyscanner or booked a hotel on Trip.com, you have used this company.

money.plain: fees on flight and train tickets

money.part: International Trip.com platform and inbound travel
money.plain: bookings by non-Chinese travellers and visitors to China

result.summary: Trip.com has a real advantage in China: Ctrip is the default app for booking hotels and flights, and its huge base of travellers and hotels feeds a network that rivals find hard to match, giving it high margins (about 81% gross and 25% operating in 2025). That strength was questioned in July 2026 when China's market regulator SAMR fined it RMB5.18 billion for abusing a dominant position over hotels, which will limit some of the tactics it used. Outside China it is a fast-growing but smaller challenger to Booking Holdings and Expedia.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin stayed around 80-82% in 2023-2025 while revenue rose from RMB44.5bn to RMB62.4bn, showing it can hold commission rates; but SAMR's July 2026 ruling found it used traffic allocation and pricing tools to force exclusive deals and lowest prices on hotels, so its leverage over suppliers is now constrained, and Meituan and Douyin compete on price for lower-tier hotels.

moats.evidence: Ctrip has been China's best-known travel booking brand since its 1999 founding, and the group also owns Skyscanner, Qunar and Trip.com.
Travellers can compare and book on Meituan, Fliggy or Booking with little effort, though Ctrip's membership tiers and corporate-travel contracts add some stickiness.
The largest pool of Chinese travellers attracts the most hotels and inventory, which in turn attracts more travellers; SAMR's 2026 decision formally found the company held a dominant market position.
With RMB62.4bn of 2025 revenue it can spend on service centres, technology and marketing more than most rivals, giving operating margins of about 25%.
Online travel is not a natural monopoly; Meituan, Tongcheng, Fliggy and Douyin all operate profitably or at scale alongside it.
Its model is the standard OTA model; no clear business model incumbents cannot copy.
Its 24/7 customer service operation and its handling of complex multi-leg and cross-border itineraries are built up over 25 years and hard to replicate quickly.
Exclusive hotel arrangements were exactly what SAMR ordered it to end in July 2026, so it has no protected exclusive asset.

customers.evidence: Ctrip is the go-to app for higher-spending Chinese travellers and its international platform revenue rose over 50% year on year in Q2 2026, but regulators and hotel associations (for example in Yunnan in December 2025) have complained about its treatment of suppliers, and no independent NPS data are published.

talent.evidence: It had 36,249 employees at end-2023, is known for pioneering hybrid work in China and announced a RMB1 billion childcare subsidy for staff in 2023, though it does not top global employer rankings.

product.evidence: Ctrip/Trip.com offers one of the broadest one-stop inventories (hotels, flights, trains, tours, car hire) in Asia, and Skyscanner is one of the most-used flight comparison sites; independent benchmarks are limited.

competitors.name: Meituan
competitors.note: Domestic hotel bookings, especially budget and lower-tier city hotels, cross-sold from its food delivery app.

competitors.name: Tongcheng Travel Holdings
competitors.note: Flight, train and hotel bookings for lower-tier city users, distributed through Tencent's WeChat.

competitors.name: Alibaba Group (Fliggy)
competitors.note: Fliggy travel marketplace for flights, hotels and packages in China.

competitors.name: ByteDance (Douyin)
competitors.note: Hotel and travel package sales through short-video and live-stream content.

competitors.name: Booking Holdings (Booking.com, Agoda)
competitors.note: Global hotel booking and Agoda in Asia, the main rival for the international Trip.com platform.

competitors.name: Expedia Group
competitors.note: International hotel, flight and package bookings.

competitors.name: Airbnb
competitors.note: Short-term rentals and homestays competing for leisure stays.

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Flights, Google Hotels)
competitors.note: Travel search and metasearch outside China, competing with Skyscanner and for traffic.

competitors.name: Traveloka
competitors.note: Online travel in Southeast Asia, a growth market for Trip.com.

competitors.name: H World Group
competitors.note: Large Chinese hotel chain pushing direct bookings through its own app and loyalty programme.

competitors.name: China State Railway Group (12306)
competitors.note: Official 12306 train ticket app and airline direct-sales channels reduce reliance on OTAs.

estimates.name: Meituan (estimate, FY2024; not an SEC filer)
Tongcheng Travel Holdings (not an SEC filer; figures not checked)

threats: SAMR's July 2026 anti-monopoly decision (RMB5.18bn in fines and confiscated gains) bars exclusive hotel deals and forced lowest-price terms, which could weaken its pricing leverage and margins.
US shareholder class action over undisclosed pricing-tool practices, and further local anti-monopoly complaints from hotel associations.
Meituan, Douyin and Tongcheng competing for lower-tier and younger travellers with heavy subsidies and content-driven sales.
Slower growth: net revenue rose only 6% year on year in Q2 2026 after 17% growth in 2025.
Geopolitical and China-economy risk affecting outbound travel and foreign investors' appetite for Chinese stocks.
AI travel agents and Google moving into direct booking could reduce traffic to OTAs internationally.

ceo.name: Jane Jie Sun
ceo.background: Business degree from the University of Florida and LLM from Peking University; former KPMG audit manager and Applied Materials reporting head; joined Ctrip as CFO in 2005

c1.evidence: It leads online travel in China, but online travel is a mature industry; growth now comes from inbound and international travel, where its international platform revenue grew over 50% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Travellers choose Ctrip for the broadest inventory and reliable 24/7 service, but SAMR's 2026 ruling showed part of its hotel price advantage came from exclusive deals it must now drop.

c3.evidence: Ctrip is a household name and the default booking app in China, but outside China Trip.com is far less known than Booking.com or Expedia.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission is "to pursue the perfect trip for a better world", and co-founder James Liang promotes travel and family policy, but the mission is rarely the centre of its communication.

c6.evidence: “convenient, dominant, reliable” are common words for Ctrip in China; the impression is mostly positive among travellers but hurt by the 2026 antitrust fine and hotel complaints.

c7.evidence: Travel is one of the largest consumer categories and Chinese outbound, inbound and international travel keep growing, lifting revenue from RMB20.0bn in 2022 to RMB62.4bn in 2025.

c8.evidence: It is expanding the Trip.com brand across Asia and Europe and building inbound-to-China travel, with international platform revenue up over 50% in Q2 2026.

m1.evidence: Jane Sun has pushed globalisation and AI-driven travel tools, but her strategy is evolutionary rather than a bold new vision.

m2.evidence: Sun is not a founder but has been with the company since 2005; co-founder James Liang remains executive chairman and sets long-term priorities such as ‘Globalization and Great Quality’.

m4.evidence: The company emphasises customer service and introduced a RMB1 billion childcare subsidy for staff in 2023, but the 2026 SAMR findings show hotel partners were treated harshly.

m5.evidence: It has a strong service and engineering culture and was an early adopter of hybrid work in China, but it is more a fast follower than an inventor of new products.

m6.evidence: Sun's background is accounting and finance (KPMG, Applied Materials, CFO), not engineering.

m7.evidence: She is widely recognised (Fortune's Most Powerful Women in Business list from 2017), but the company was fined in 2026 for abusing its dominant position.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Jane Sun at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: She is a respected but low-profile executive without a distinctive public persona.

m9.evidence: Since she became CEO in November 2016 the company came through COVID and grew revenue to a record RMB62.4bn in 2025 with a 25% operating margin.

m10.evidence: No well-known frugality culture is documented.

c10.evidence: It makes travel booking easier for hundreds of millions of people in China and Asia, but booking travel is a convenience rather than a life-changing need.

p2.evidence: Running a global one-stop travel platform with service centres is hard, but many rivals do similar things.

f1.evidence: Net revenue rose every year from RMB18.3bn in 2020 to RMB20.0bn, RMB20.0bn, RMB44.5bn, RMB53.3bn and RMB62.4bn in 2025.

f2.evidence: Operating margin went from -7.8% in 2020 to 25.3% in 2025 and gross margin from 78.0% to 80.6%, though both have eased slightly since 2024.

f3.evidence: At 30 June 2026 cash and short-term investments of RMB79.5bn far exceeded debt of RMB26.4bn, and shareholders' equity was RMB160.7bn.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from a RMB1.4bn loss in 2020 to RMB15.8bn in 2025, with operating cash flow recovering strongly after COVID.

v1.evidence: In China Ctrip is the clear choice for higher-end and complex trips thanks to breadth and service; internationally Booking.com and Agoda have more inventory.

v2.evidence: It is known for family-friendly policies, but no top global employer ranking was found.

c5.evidence: Chinese travellers and hotels relying on its traffic would miss it, but Meituan, Fliggy and Tongcheng could largely replace it.
